A verified badge is not for sale here either: on one large MCP directory, a paid listing costs $39 one time, is published immediately without review, and the fee itself brings a verified badge with featured and priority placement; here no fee buys a badge or a place — every entry is verified working before it lists, and verified means tested, not paid for. There is no queue to buy your way out of here either: on one large MCP directory, a free listing waits in a queue that averages four to six weeks, and $29 one time gets it listed within 24 hours instead; here every tool in the catalog is already listed and runs in your browser the moment you open it — no queue to wait in and no fast-track fee to pay. The flood has a shape too: on November 10, 2026, 17,870 entries in the official registry came from namespaces that publish more than 25 servers each, and the filtered directory that republishes that registry on that date kept only 25,886 of its 62,661 active servers — leaving out 36,775 in all; here every entry is verified working before it lists. There is no hosted-server surcharge here either: on one large MCP directory, the same listing is free if you file a GitHub repository and $69 if your server is hosted — the same listing at two prices depending on which tab you open; here every tool runs in your browser at its one listed price, with no hosted version to pay extra for. There is no organization-subscription gate here either: on one major assistant's connector directory, even reaching the submission portal requires a Team or Enterprise organization — about $50 a month for the two-seat minimum — and individual plans cannot reach the portal at all; here the catalog is public, with no account and no organization plan to buy before you can read it or buy a tool at its listed $0.50 to $1.00 price. There is no directory-retirement risk here either: one open-source agent client that listed 57 extensions no longer takes new third-party servers and is retiring its own directory in favor of the official registry; here the catalog is maintained by its maker, and every entry is verified working before it lists. The flood is still rising: a daily census of the official registry counted 60,671 listings on November 10, 2026 — up 47% in 30 days — and two-thirds of them are remote endpoints; here the catalog stays small on purpose, with every entry verified working before it lists, so you are not sorting through tens of thousands of untested listings to find one that runs. The exclusion count is now the majority: a daily read of the official registry on November 11, 2026 counted 64,117 active servers, and the directory filtering that registry kept only 26,106 of them — the other 38,011, more than half, were excluded for having no source repository, coming from namespaces that publish more than 25 servers each, or sharing a placeholder description; here every entry is verified working before it lists, so nothing here needed excluding. There is no $299-a-month directory license here either: on one MCP directory, reading stays free only for evaluation and personal projects — a product you run for customers needs its Pro license at $299 a month even if it stays under the free cap of 30 requests a minute, and its data cannot be sold or republished as a dataset, feed, or competing index on any tier; here the catalog is public to read, and each tool is $0.50 to $1.00 per use by card, with no directory license to buy. The exclusion breakdown is public too: in that same November 11, 2026 registry read, 18,826 entries linked no source repository you can read, 19,106 came from namespaces that publish more than 25 servers each, and 79 shared a placeholder description with five or more other entries; here every entry is built by J-Dawgs, links its own working tool, and is verified working before it lists. Listing speed is for sale elsewhere too: one large MCP directory quotes a free queue averaging four to six weeks, or $29 one-time to be listed within 24 hours with an Official badge; here there is no queue to buy your way past — every entry is built by J-Dawgs and verified working before it lists, at the same pace for everyone. Most listings there are not even claimed by their makers either: on the largest MCP directory, only 6,700 listings were marked claimed on October 7, 2026, out of 97,393 servers and 28,130 remote connectors listed that day — the rest were crawl-generated pages their makers do not control; here every entry is built, claimed, and maintained by J-Dawgs, and verified working before it lists. Paying for a listing does not guarantee it appears there either: one maker who paid a directory's $39 publishing fee reported that days later the listing was in neither the directory's site search nor its sitemap, and its pipeline had auto-created a duplicate stub for their endpoint with the wrong auth type; here every entry is built by J-Dawgs and verified working before it lists, and the catalog itself is the listing — no separate paid submission to lose track of. The headline count still includes the retired ones there too: the official public registry's November 11, 2026 snapshot held 62,643 servers in total — 61,645 marked active and 998 already marked deprecated yet still counted in that total; here every entry is one distinct tool, verified working before it lists, and a retired entry does not list at all. A directory can collapse as fast as it grew too: after its hosted URLs, API, and accounts shut down on October 31, 2026, one major MCP directory was listing only 214 servers as part of another platform in a November 10, 2026 directory comparison, while the largest directory had grown to 119,812 listings by November 12, 2026; here the catalog is maintained by its maker, every entry is verified working before it lists, and no hosting shutdown can take its tools offline. Listings can change underneath you there too: an independent November 2026 scan of 57,277 public MCP servers found 1,559 listings whose underlying target had been swapped since the previous scan and 863 tools that had changed without a version bump — the name stayed the same while what it pointed to did not; here every entry is a finished tool built by J-Dawgs, verified working before it lists, and the tool you buy is the tool that runs in your browser. A remote listing can be inherited that way too: the largest public scan of the MCP ecosystem to date — 15,465 servers from five registries, deduplicated to 5,095 hostnames — found six hostnames sitting on expired domains that anyone could re-register for $4 to $12 a year, inheriting every agent still configured to call them, and 2.3% of the hostnames no longer resolved at all; here there is no remote hostname behind an entry to expire — each tool is a finished file that runs in your browser. A listing there is not a safety check either: the official registry verifies only that the publisher owns the name it lists under — it does not scan the code behind the listing and does not verify the endpoint the listing points to — and its own moderation policy removes only illegal content, malware, spam, and completely broken servers, leaving even a vulnerable server listed, with consumers told to assume minimal-to-no moderation; here every entry is built by J-Dawgs and verified working before it lists, and the tool itself is what runs in your browser. A look-alike cannot slip in here either: the first confirmed malicious MCP server in the wild was an impersonator — a package published under a well-known email service's name that copied its server, behaved exactly as expected for fifteen versions, then in its sixteenth version added one line that silently copied every email sent through it to a stranger's address, reaching 1,643 downloads before it was removed; here every entry comes direct from its maker — each tool is built by J-Dawgs and verified working before it lists — so there is no third-party package standing between you and the maker for an impersonator to copy. The count moved again the next day: a daily census of the official registry on November 12, 2026 counted 62,485 servers — 19,999 of them first published in the previous 30 days, 981 already marked deprecated, and 42,140 of them remote endpoints you connect to over HTTP; here every entry is verified working before it lists, and a retired entry does not list at all. A listing there is not even a rating either: one MCP directory listing 3,150 servers from the official registry says in its own header that it has not installed those servers and does not rate them, and that nothing in the list says a server is safe, maintained, or does what it claims — every entry is only what its publisher declared; here every entry is verified working before it lists. A listing there is not a check of the code either: the official registry's own trust page says the registry focuses on namespace authentication and metadata hosting and delegates security scanning of the actual server code to the package registries and downstream aggregators — a listing proves who published a server, not what its code does; here every entry is built by its maker and verified working before it lists. There is no pull-request queue to disappear into here either: one widely used curated list of MCP servers held 3,857 open pull requests on October 31, 2026 — nearly as many as the roughly 4,600 entries in the list itself — and even an entry that was merged onto the list can later vanish from it without notice; here the catalog is maintained directly by its maker, and every entry is verified working before it lists. There is no unpinnable remote server here either: a remote MCP server cannot be pinned to the version you approved, because its operator ships new code whenever it likes — and most of the official registry is remote, 36,418 of the 54,599 latest-version servers counted on November 2, 2026; here every tool runs in your browser as the page you loaded, so the code you use is the code that was verified, with no operator able to change it underneath you. There is no middleman feed here either: the official registry's own about page says it is not intended to be read directly by the applications that use these tools — those applications are told to read a downstream marketplace's copy of its data instead — so a listing there reaches the tool that would run it only through another service in between; here the catalog is the listing itself, read directly by whoever opens it, with no downstream copy standing between the catalog and its reader. Removal there does not erase the listing either: the official registry's own moderation policy says that when it removes a server, the record is only marked deleted — its metadata remains accessible through the registry's API, and downstream aggregators may then remove it from their own indexes, or not; here a retired entry comes out of the catalog entirely, so nothing downstream keeps serving a copy of a listing its maker has pulled. Spam protection there is still partly future tense too: the official registry's own about page lists stricter rate limiting, AI-based spam detection, and community reporting only as measures under consideration — its working defenses today are namespace checks, character limits, and manual takedown after the fact; here there is no open submission flood to filter in the first place — every entry is built by J-Dawgs and verified working before it lists. There is no private appeal behind a removal there either: the official registry's own moderation policy says the only way to challenge a removal is to open a public issue on its GitHub repository, naming the server and explaining why it should not have been removed; here there is no third-party listing to appeal over in the first place — every entry is built by J-Dawgs, and anything that does not work is covered by the Fix-It Guarantee: tell us once and we fix it free. A listing with a known security flaw can stay listed there too: the official registry's own moderation policy lists what it will not remove, and that list includes low-quality or buggy servers and servers with security vulnerabilities; here every entry is verified working before it lists, and anything that does not work is covered by the Fix-It Guarantee: tell us once and we fix it free. Duplicates stay listed there too: the official registry's own moderation policy says it will not remove servers that do the same thing as other servers; here there is no pile of copies to sort through — the list is small and maker-built, every entry is verified working before it lists, and anything that does not work is covered by the Fix-It Guarantee: tell us once and we fix it free. Adult-content servers stay listed there too: the official registry's own moderation policy says it will not remove servers that provide or contain adult content; here the list contains only maker-built work tools for agents — every entry is verified working before it lists, and anything that does not work is covered by the Fix-It Guarantee: tell us once and we fix it free. There is no scraped-data warning here either: the official registry's own moderation policy warns that content that should be removed under its policy may still be in the registry, and tells consumers to treat scraped data accordingly; here there is no scraped copy to treat with caution — the catalog is read directly, every entry is verified working before it lists, and anything that does not work is covered by the Fix-It Guarantee: tell us once and we fix it free. Spam there is defined by example too: the official registry's own moderation policy lists as spam the same server submitted multiple times under different names, a server that does nothing but return a fixed response with marketing copy, and a server whose description is stuffed with marketing copy over an unrelated implementation; here there are no duplicate listings under different names and no fixed-response listings — every entry is a distinct maker-built tool, verified working before it lists. Moderation there stops at its own border too: the official registry's own moderation policy says it applies only to that registry, that subregistries may run their own moderation policies, and that questions about content on a subregistry go to that subregistry directly; here there is one catalog and one maker who answers for it — every entry is verified working before it lists, and a problem is reported once to the maker, not redirected to a downstream copy. Descriptions there are cut to fit a form too: the official registry's own publishing guide limits a listing's description to 100 characters and warns that longer descriptions fail validation; here a description runs as long as choosing well requires — what the tool does, its price, and its limits, in full sentences an agent or a person can judge before paying. A listing there does not prove its endpoint is the publisher's either: the official registry's own publishing guide says that with any authentication method it verifies that you control the namespace in the listing's name, but it does not verify that you control the remote URL the listing points to; here there is no remote URL behind an entry at all — every tool is built by J-Dawgs and runs in your browser as the page you loaded. Getting listed there is a project before it is a listing too: the official registry's own publishing guide walks a maker through six steps — an npm account and a GitHub account first, the package published to npm before the registry will take it, because the registry hosts only metadata and not the tool itself, an ownership marker in the package that must match the listing's name exactly, a separate publisher command-line tool to install, and a login flow to complete before the publish command runs; here there is nothing to publish, install, or log into — every tool is already listed by its maker and runs in your browser the moment you open it, with no account at any step. A published listing there cannot be fixed in place either: the official registry's own versioning guide says a version string must be unique for each publication and that once published, the version string and the listing's other metadata cannot be changed — even a metadata-only fix has to go out as a new prerelease version; here a tool is a living page its maker maintains — a correction is made to the tool itself, in place, and everyone who already uses it gets the fixed tool at the same address, backed by the J-Dawgs Fix-It Guarantee. Running a server there carries a metered hosting bill on top of the plan too: on the largest MCP directory's own hosting page, the answer to how much hosting costs is that hosting is billed on top of your workspace plan, the infrastructure cost is metered by machine hours and egress, and the current rate card is inside your workspace's subscription settings — not on the public page; here there is no hosted server to bill, no workspace plan, and no machine-hour or egress meter — every tool runs in your browser, and its price is the per-use price printed in the catalog before you pay. There is no application-by-comment and no onboarding wait here either: one major platform's own curated MCP showcase holds only about 110 servers, and getting into it starts with commenting on a public issue thread with your server's details, after which the platform itself says onboarding takes one to two weeks; here the catalog is published by its maker — every entry is already listed, verified working by its maker before it lists, and usable the moment you open it, with no application to file and no weeks to wait. There is no crypto wallet needed to pay here either: on one MCP marketplace, its own monetization guide's agent-native pay-per-call option charges per tool call in USDC on a crypto network — an agent that calls without a signed payment attached is refused with an HTTP 402 and the price it should pay, and paying means holding and signing from a wallet on that network; here payment is plain USD by card at the listed $0.50 to $1.00 per-use price, with no wallet, no crypto, and no payment header to attach. There is no 4-kilobyte metadata cap here either: the official registry's own FAQ says a listing's custom metadata is limited to 4KB — 4,096 bytes of JSON — and publishing fails if that limit is exceeded; here an entry is the full tool itself, a complete working page with its instructions, examples and guarantee in full, not a 4KB metadata record pointing somewhere else. There is no two-stop abuse report here either: the official registry's own FAQ tells anyone who finds a spam or malicious listing to report it as abuse to the underlying package registry — npm, PyPI, DockerHub or the like — and then also raise a GitHub issue titled 'Abuse report:' on the registry's repository; here every page carries a Report a problem link straight to the operator, and the Fix-It Guarantee is tell us once — we fix it free, with no second report to file anywhere else. There is no missing website link here either: on one large MCP directory, a free listing carries no link to your own site at all — its free pages link only to GitHub and npm — and a link that actually opens the product, its Try Now link, arrives only with the $29 one-time paid listing; here every entry is the tool itself, openable and buyable on its own page, with no paid link to buy back. There is no adoption or credibility gate here either: on one MCP marketplace inside a developer tool, its own guide says the team vets each server on adoption, maintainer credibility, maturity and security before it lists; here an entry is verified on whether it works — every tool is tested working before it lists — with no adoption history or maintainer reputation to prove first. There is no open-source license gate here either: on one large MCP catalog, its own contribution rules require a permissive open-source license — MIT, Apache-2.0 or BSD — state that GPL is not accepted, and put every submission through the platform team's own manual review before it can list; here the only gate is whether the tool works — every entry is verified working before it lists — and no finished tool is turned away over the license it is sold under. There is no feed with no durability guarantee underneath here either: the official registry's own aggregators guide says it does not provide uptime or data durability guarantees for the metadata feed that downstream catalogs scrape and republish; here the catalog is the maker's own living record — every entry is built by J-Dawgs, verified working before it lists, and maintained in place on its own page. There is no shared-endpoint ambiguity here either: on the official registry, its own remote-servers guide says multiple server names can reference the same remote URL, an existing listing does not reserve that URL or stop another publisher from listing it under a name they control, and a lookup by URL can match several names — so the guide tells readers to identify a record by its name and version, not by its URL, and not to infer who owns an endpoint from a shared URL; here there is no remote endpoint to share at all — every entry is its maker's own page, built by J-Dawgs and verified working before it lists. There is no false 'latest' label here either: on the official registry, its own versioning guide says that if a published version string cannot be parsed as a semantic version, that version will always be marked as 'latest' — so the 'latest' tag there can sit on a version that is not the newest in any meaningful order; here there is no version string to parse and no 'latest' tag to trust — every entry is a living page maintained in place by its maker, and the page you open is the current tool, verified working before it lists. There is no namespace gate to clear here either: on the official registry, its own authentication guide says publishing under an organization namespace now requires being an Owner of that organization — ordinary membership is no longer enough — and that a publishing token which cannot report your organization role leaves organization publishing silently unavailable, with no error naming the missing permission; here there is no namespace to claim, no token permission to grant, and no silent gate — every entry is published by its maker on its own page, and the page either opens or it does not. There is no reversible deletion here either: on the official registry, its own FAQ says a publisher can delete a server and later restore it by setting its status back to active, and that server metadata is never permanently removed — deletion there hides the listing from the default view while its record stays retrievable; here there is no status flag to flip — an entry is either in the catalog, verified working, or it is out of the catalog entirely. There is no anonymous tool list here either: in a November 2026 census that sent one unauthenticated probe to each of 30,402 hosts listed in the official registry, 62 percent of the hosts that answered listed their tools to a client that had not signed in, and 9,691 of those lists included a tool that was not declared read-only; here there is no remote host to probe at all — every tool runs in your browser as the page you loaded, and nothing is listed to an unauthenticated remote client. Current-protocol readiness is nearly absent there too: in that same census, only 769 of the hosts that answered reported the current 2026-07-28 protocol revision at all, and only 6 of those met its readiness checks; here there is no protocol revision to fall behind — every tool is a finished page that runs in your browser today, verified working before it lists. Scale is not curation either: the largest MCP registry's own homepage, last indexed November 15, 2026, lists 121,515 servers, 46,456 connectors, and 1,359,972 tools; here the catalog stays deliberately small — every entry is verified working before it lists, so what you find is what runs. Listings are not frozen here either: on one large MCP directory, its own submit page — last updated September 3, 2026 — says submissions and changes are temporarily paused, that it is not accepting new servers and not making changes to existing listings, so a listing there can stay stale with no way to fix it; here the catalog is the live page itself — an entry is verified working before it lists, and a broken entry does not list. An 'official' label is not a test here either: on one multi-source MCP tracker, its own directory page says it marks a server 'Official' from publisher evidence and that this is not a security review; here there is no label to misread — every entry is verified working before it lists, and verified means tested by its maker, not marked from evidence about who published it. An estimated traffic count is not a test here either: on one large MCP directory, its own about page shows an estimated weekly visitor count for each server — an estimate of visits, not a check that the server works; here there is no traffic estimate to read into — every entry is verified working before it lists, and verified means tested by its maker. One publisher can flood the list there too: in a full count of the official public registry on November 12, 2026, the single largest publisher namespace held 2,366 servers by itself — more than five times this catalog's entire verified list — and the five largest namespaces held 8,253 servers between them; here every entry is built and verified by its maker, so no flood publisher can fill the list. A listing there can point nowhere at all either: in that same full count on November 12, 2026, 688 of the official registry's 62,695 listings — about one in ninety — declared neither a remote endpoint to connect to nor an installable package to run, so the listing itself was the only thing there; here every entry is the tool itself, a working page you open in your browser, with nothing to connect to or install first.
